prompt: The internet has made possible for everybody to read anything online for free. This will make it unnecessary to pay for printed materials such as books or newspapers in the future. To what extent do you agree or disagree with this statement? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
essay:
On the topic of whether the abundance and accessibility of digital media makes paying for print mediums redundant, I strongly disagree. While the internet provides a plethora of resources, habitual usage of physical media will ensure their enduring existence.

Admittedly, the vast amount of free resources available online might pose a threat to the relevance of print media. In a world in which almost anything can be found online, from news to novels, the continued existence of books could be questioned. There is a certain amount of convenience in not having to visit a physical store, in order to acquire new reading materials. It might also be beneficial for people who have to commute to work to carry less weight around. Plenty of different books and articles can be assembled on one e-reader. But when it comes to the question of whether those materials are inherently cheaper or even free, I would have to disagree. Most articles are hidden behind paywalls nowadays and e-books on the most common sites like “Apple Books” appear to increase in price dramatically as inflation continues to rise.

On the other side of the equation are habitual readers. These people are notoriously drawn to the qualities of real paper, such as the feel and even the scent. Avid readers nowadays often fall into one of two categories: young and enamoured with the concept and romanticism of reading as much as with the books themselves, and elderly with a long standing habit of reading the newspaper. Plenty of my friends read for both content and aesthetics. The publishing industry is very aware of this trend, selling specially bound editions that look deliberately pretty. The market for those books is flourishing despite the higher prices. Social media niches such as “Book-Tok” or “Book-Tube” have long since become instrumental in marketing- not only books, but an entire lifestyle centred around being a reader. Conversely, the older generations are creatures of habit. Many of my geriatric patients prefer to read the local newspaper over breakfast. I would earn a lot of dismay, if I were to suggest that they read online instead. And that does not even touch upon the matter of accessibility, which has been proven in a 2021 study from Copenhagen to plummet after a certain age range. As a digital native, it is hard to comprehend, but I experienced firsthand that digital media are not unlike learning a new language or advanced arithmetic for the elderly population.

For these reasons, a lack of accessibility for all age groups and ingrained habits with inherent marketability in most avid readers, I believe that books and newspapers will never be made redundant by online media. This statement holds despite the modern conveniences and cost saving potential that digital media bring to the table.
